entries.content:
How Databricks brings governed context, your business ontology, and fast AI decision making together to tailor every customer conversation in real time.

*Voice is already changing how customers interact with brands. People who moved from storefronts to websites to apps now expect to simply talk to the companies they buy from, and the same shift is reaching suppliers, drivers, and field teams.

*Most enterprise AI so far has faced inward. The larger opportunity is in the conversations companies have with customers and partners every day, and each of those conversations can now be captured, understood, and acted on in real time.

*Any team can build a voice agent that talks back, but value is created only when the agent has context on who is calling. From there, it can adapt to that person, stay within set rules, and get better with every call.

*On Databricks, the agent's brain sits next to your governed data. Context and ontology ground every answer, fast AI decisions tailor each turn, and every call feeds a learning loop.

*Getting started is straightforward. Pick one high-volume routine call, measure how well the agent handles it, and use the DIVA blueprint as the starting point for the next one.

Consider three moments that happen every day in consumer businesses:

  • At 6 a.m., a driver running late for a delivery window calls dispatch to move his dock appointment. He’s behind the wheel, so an app isn’t an option. Three other drivers are already on hold, and every minute he waits puts the next delivery at risk.
  • At noon, a drive-thru has four cars in line and one employee on the headset, who is also taking payment and handing out orders. Guests can only order by speaking, so the line moves only as fast as one employee can facilitate orders.
  • In the evening, a storm grounds flights, and stranded travelers call their hotel to hold rooms and push back arrivals. Standing at a gate with a bag in each hand, a phone call is easier and faster than a website. The reservations team has two people and forty calls coming in.

In each of these moments, voice is the fastest or only way the customer can reach the business. So if voice ultimately serves the customer and business need most effectively, why is it so often not available or, in more recent times, executed poorly?

For years, the answer was that voice was too hard to get right. That is no longer true. Synthetic voices now sound natural, a conversation can be turned into text and acted on while the caller is still on the line, and today's voice agents can keep pace with the roughly 200 milliseconds it typically takes people to answer each other in conversation.

What has not caught up is how most companies think about it. Enterprise AI investment has largely faced inward, toward assistants for employees, while the larger opportunity sits in the conversations companies have with customers and partners every day. One of the largest quick-service restaurant brands in the United States is already building toward exactly that, with a voice agent that lets guests add items to their cart, change their order, and check out simply by talking.

Example use cases where voice agents can create value.

Every one of these calls, from the driver moving a dock appointment to the traveler holding a room after a storm, depends on more than understanding speech. To be useful, the agent needs the same context your best employee would have: who is calling, what is already in motion for them, and what it is allowed to do about it.

Most voice agent pilots prove that an agent can hold a conversation. Far fewer prove that it can be trusted with a real customer. Context closes that gap. With it, the agent can adapt to each caller, stay within your rules about what it can see and say, and get better with every call. Without it, even the most natural voice can only give generic answers.

Consider a single call. A loyal customer phones about a late order. The agent already knows who they are, what they ordered, and where the package is. It apologizes, offers a loyalty credit it is authorized to give, and arranges a replacement. If the customer is still frustrated, the agent picks up on it in the moment and decides, in a fraction of a second, to route the call to the next available person. That person picks up with the full context, so the customer neither waits in a queue nor repeats themselves. The same pattern holds when a patient moves an appointment or a subscriber cannot log in after a charge they don't recognize. In each case, the agent picks up when the customer steps away from the app or website and needs an answer now, then hands them back to that same journey when the call is done.

Pulling that context together on a live call is the real challenge. It lives across many systems, the agent needs it in a fraction of a second, and it has to stay governed the whole time. That is where Databricks comes in.

A voice agent has two parts. The first is the conversation layer, which handles the call itself: carrying the audio, turning speech into text, and speaking the reply. Specialist partners do this well. In our prototype, LiveKit carries the call, Deepgram handles speech-to-text and the default voice, and ElevenLabs adds expressive voices. Phone carriers such as Twilio can bring in regular phone lines.

The second part is the brain, which Databricks provides. On every turn of the call, it looks up the caller’s context, applies your business rules, and chooses the next step, whether that means answering a question, making an offer, or handing the call to a person. It also records each decision so your teams can review it later. The conversation layer shapes how the agent sounds. The brain decides whether it gets the answer right.

The brain stands on a foundation of three things that already live together on Databricks.

  • Context is the data the agent needs at the moment: the customer, order, product, and policy data that belongs to the person on the line.
  • Ontology is how that data connects. It captures the definitions and relationships your business runs on, such as what makes someone a loyalty member, which store an order belongs to, and which policy applies to which product, so the agent can reason about your business the way your employees do.
  • Governance decides who can see what. On Databricks, an AI agent follows the same access rules in your enterprise data catalog that your employees already follow.

For Databricks customers, there is no new platform to stand up. The agent runs where your data already lives and connects to the systems you already run, such as ordering, loyalty, and CRM, through approved, read-only lookups.

During a customer interaction, the agent uses your context and ontology to look up this person’s orders, your policies, and your product information, so every answer reflects your business rather than general knowledge from the internet. The agent only sees the records that belong to the caller, and it confirms who they are by checking your systems rather than taking their word for it. Your business decides which offers the agent can make, how much credit it can give, and the point at which a person takes over.

If the agent cannot find the answer in your data, it tells the caller so and transfers them to a person rather than guessing. Every answer it does give can be traced back to the record it came from. Sensitive topics, such as medical, financial, or safety questions, are routed to a human by design, and the agent is built never to give medical advice. Only the conversation passes through speech partners, and customer data stays on your governed platform.

A voice agent needs two kinds of thinking. Some decisions have to happen in a fraction of a second, like whether a driver with a dock problem or an upset caller should go to a person right now. Others need careful reasoning, like working out the right fix for a delayed order. Researchers call this fast and slow thinking, or System 1 and System 2, and AI is now being built the same way. Large language models (System 2) do the careful reasoning, while a new class of fast decision models (System 1), such as Jev from TypeSafe AI, handles the quick calls. Databricks brings System 1 decision making to your governed data with ai_decide, so the agent can make a quick call and show how confident it is.

In a voice agent, the two work side by side on every turn of the conversation.

  • A loyal member or returning guest gets their full history and the offers they qualify for, backed by your most capable model, while a routine question gets a quick, accurate answer at lower cost.
  • An upset caller is handed to a person, along with the order or reservation, any earlier complaints, and any offers already made.
  • A caller who switches languages hears the agent switch with them.
  • A subscriber who sees a charge they don't recognize and can't log in is verified against your records and moved straight to account recovery, instead of waiting in a general queue.
  • A subscriber who calls to cancel hears the save offer they actually qualify for, at the moment it can still change their mind.
  • A patient who asks whether a symptom is serious is transferred to a nurse with the full transcript.
  • A driver reporting a dock incident is escalated immediately, before it costs you a shipment.

This lets you use your most capable models where they make a real difference to the customer, and faster, lower-cost models for everything else.

Every one of those decisions is recorded. With caller consent and recording disclosure handled at the phone layer, each call can be captured in one governed place: what was said, what was looked up, which model answered, and why each decision was made. Your teams control who can access those records and how long they are kept, using the same policies that already govern the rest of your data. The agent inherits the Databricks platform's security and compliance programs, including HIPAA and SOC 2 Type II options, described in the Databricks Trust Center. Speech partners carry their own certifications that need to be reviewed as part of your rollout.

That record is what lets the agent improve. Every call can be scored for quality automatically, and contact center and customer experience leaders can ask questions about their calls in natural language, such as why refund requests spiked last Tuesday. Those insights can then be fed back into better prompts and models, further improving the effectiveness of the voice agent.

Getting started does not require a large program. The building blocks are available today, and the Databricks Intelligent Voice Agents (DIVA) blueprint, which is open source on GitHub, gives your teams a working starting point. Voice then becomes a new channel on top of the systems you already have.

The voice agent is there to take on the routine calls that fill the queue, such as order status, refills, and rebookings, so your staff can focus on the conversations that need a human: an upset customer, a complex request, or a caller who would simply rather talk to a person. When a staff member picks up, the full history is already on their screen, and if anything goes wrong, the call moves to a person with the full transcript.

This is where customer service is heading. Gartner predicts that by 2029, agentic AI will autonomously resolve 80% of common customer service issues without human intervention, leading to a 30% reduction in operational costs.

Databricks industry engineers recommend starting with a 90-day pilot that covers one channel, one team, and your highest-volume routine call, such as order status, a driver check-in, or a supplier confirmation. Before the pilot begins, record today's cost per call, handle time, and customer satisfaction, and track whether callers come back and buy again, so you can compare the results at the end. Once the results hold up, you can extend the same governed setup to more locations and more types of calls.

Three questions for your next leadership meeting

  • Which customer and partner conversations do we handle most often, and which of them could an agent answer accurately today?
  • If a voice agent answered on our behalf tomorrow, would it know who it was talking to, and would it follow the same rules as our employees?
  • Can we trace every decision an agent makes on a call and show that it was governed?

To see it in action, watch the full demo and share the DIVA blueprint on GitHub with your technical team. It includes ready-made instructions that coding agents can follow. Then reach out to your Databricks account team to discuss and brainstorm your first use case.

Your customers will soon be talking to an AI agent on your behalf. What matters is how well that agent knows them.

entries.content:
Accelerate healthcare and life sciences workflows with AI coding and skills

by Zachary Phillips, May Merkle-Tan, Praneeth Paikray, Peter Hawkins, Vimal Thomas Joseph, Rohan Parikh and Yen Low

  • What: Vital Skills skills are open-source Agent Skills that give coding agents healthcare and life sciences (HLS) domain expertise. In particular, Genie Code, optimized for the full-featured Databricks platform, further benefits from the HLS-specific guidance to apply domain tools and best practices.
  • Problem: General agents write plausible code but lack domain discipline. They pick clinical thresholds silently and opt for generic statistical methods instead of specialized ones that are de rigueur in the domain.
  • Results: On BiomniBench (an assessment tool for large language model (LLM) agents used in biomedical research), Genie Code with Vital Skills scored higher on in-scope tasks that the skills supported compared to Genie Code alone. Overall, we found that Vital Skills improved consistency, accuracy and rigor. Fewer steps and checks were missed. There were fewer retries and the tools were more likely to follow the industry standard.

Genie Code, our coding agent optimized for Databricks, allows you to chat instead of code to perform your data and AI tasks. Critically, Genie Code’s integration with Unity Catalog ensures that the agent understands your enterprise’s data and follows the same security and governance rules as the rest of the Databricks platform. Thus, Genie Code significantly outperforms a leading coding agent by more than twice on real-world data tasks such as exploratory data analysis, machine/deep learning, creating dashboards, agents, apps, declarative automation bundles, Lakeflow jobs and scheduling them.

However, Genie Code and other general AI coding assistants lack domain specificity and assume generic methods and clinical thresholds that do not meet healthcare and life sciences (HLS) standards or best practices.

Databricks Vital Skills bridges this gap by providing packaged playbooks built in the open Agent Skills standard. They equip AI coding agents with industry knowledge so agents know which questions to ask, which steps are non-negotiable, and which tested tools to use.

Vital Skills is designed for Genie Code to make the best use of the unified Databricks ecosystem so generated code is not disconnected from your governed data, and you're not left to stand up serving, GPUs, governance, and scheduling yourself. You get a system, not just a sandbox. With the Databricks ecosystem, you:

  • Are grounded in all your data assets. The quality of the answer rises with the reach of the data foundation underneath it.
  • Are governed end to end. Data, skills, and models with conversational access are all governed, tracked and secured.
  • Get a comprehensive platform. Model Serving, GPUs, and Apps are part of the platform, with no separate software or service to buy and wire together.
  • Have open choice. Use any cloud, any model, any framework.
  • Design for production, not just play. The same work in prototype can be promoted into scheduled Lakeflow pipelines and jobs with real throughput.

We tested Genie Code with and without Vital Skills on BiomniBench, a public benchmark of biomedical data-analysis tasks graded against expert-written rubrics. Genie Code alone rarely failed on the obvious parts.

It parsed documents and generated charts with ease. However, it sometimes fell short on domain-specific methodology and knowledge and was prone to overassumptions. With Vital Skills, Genie Code scored higher on the relevant tasks and had no negative impact on tasks that were out of scope of Vital Skills.

Each skill started with a field engineer who had solved the problem several times with customers. We held on to three principles:

  • Ask before assuming. When a decision is the analyst’s to make, e.g. a clinical threshold, the skill pauses, provides options, and lets the user choose.
  • Trust-tested tools, not improvised code. For sensitive work, Genie Code runs tested tools and code rather than writing new logic each time.
  • Prove it. Every skill was run side by side against Genie Code without it, on the same tasks.

Vital Skills puts the know-how of a biostatistician, privacy officer, bioinformatician, or actuary directly in the hands of every analyst, helping teams move faster before engaging additional expertise. The Databricks Healthcare and Life Sciences field team has built skills across the industry, covering key steps in data processing, analysis, model life cycle management, evaluation, report and slide generation.

These skills can be used directly, or further customized to your needs and to leverage your deep expertise in your discipline. We expect this starter set of skills to grow over time and welcome contributions to the open source repository.

Skill What it does
Bioinformatics 
bulk-rnaseq
 Find top differentially expressed genes from bulk RNA-seq counts. 
open-weight-models
 Package, register, validate & deploy open-weight HLS models on Databricks, e.g. TEDDY and Geneformer. 
pathway-enrichment-analysis
 Pathway enrichment for RNA-seq (ORA or GSEA). 
sc-rnaseq
 Analyze single-cell RNA-seq data from .h5ad files.
Clinical 
cohort-builder
 Build a reproducible, feasibility-checked patient cohort from coded + free-text clinical data. 
rwe-cohortstudy
 Comparative effectiveness (cohort study) with propensity adjustment (matching, IPW). 
semantic-builder
 Build a semantic layer like Metric Views using 64 common measures from EHR or claims so they are dashboard or agent ready 
phi-deidentifier
 HIPAA Safe-Harbor de-identify a Unity Catalog table (k-anonymity + governed view).
Others 
presentation-builder
 Build presentation-ready slides 
report-writer
 Move your analysis methods and results to a report 
accelerators
 Route to a relevant HLS accelerator or library with the right tools for your task 
skill-eval
 Benchmark a skill: paired runs with/without it, MLflow genai.evaluate scoring, win/loss + failure taxonomy.

Go from data to a finished report or agent or dashboard seamlessly on Databricks.

For example, our semantic-builder skill defines and computes commonly used metrics (e.g. length of stay) into a Metric View from claims or electronic health records. Once Metric Views are defined in Unity Catalog, you can easily re-use them across multiple tools like dashboards, Genie Agents, external BI or spreadsheets.

In the following sections, we will dive into a couple of key skills.

An analyst describes a population in plain language — "patients with type 2 diabetes and uncontrolled blood sugar" — and the skill turns that into a cohort they can reproduce, explain, and defend. Cohort building is an integral starting point for nearly every analytics effort: RWE studies, clinical-trial feasibility, payer care-management and population-health outcomes research.

  • It works with structured and/or unstructured data. It finds patients in coded records (diagnoses, labs, medications) and optionally, in free-text notes and scanned PDFs.
  • It stops to ask at key decision points instead of guessing: which lab value counts as "uncontrolled," how to combine structured and unstructured data, and whether to deliver a table, a notebook, or an answer right in the conversation.
  • It checks feasibility first, showing how many patients qualify before building anything.
  • It explains its logic. Each patient comes with the reason they were included, without exposing raw clinical notes in the shareable result.
  • It consistently gives the same answer. In our tests it produced the same cohort on every run; Genie Code without the skill picked a different definition each time. In paired evaluations, free-text cohort F1 rose from 0.62 to 1.00.

After building cohorts, consider comparative effectiveness studies and share your results using the presentation-builder.

Some of the most promising AI applications for life sciences are open source biological foundation models that encode single-cell transcriptomics (Geneformer, scGPT, Scimilarity, TEDDY) or protein structure (AlphaFold/OpenFold, Boltz2, etc). They are also difficult to get running, requiring specialized infrastructure and abilities. Because this skill summons the appropriate code, libraries and GPU serving, a scientist can go from “I need this model" to serving a governed model that one can actually use.

Along the way it:

  • Asks rather than guess (e.g. how should the model run: a real-time endpoint, batch job, app, or pipeline) so it can deploy the model accordingly with reasoning.
  • Makes the model reproducible and auditable by pinning the model and its artifacts (e.g. code, weights, reference databases, and licenses)
  • Serves a governed model that is registered in Unity Catalog, deployed, and tested with realistic scientific inputs before handoff.
  • Monitors model traffic in inference and system tables for usage/cost tracking and optionally applies sensitive data guardrails.

On a TEDDY single-cell model deployment task, Genie Code without the skill wrote correct code but missed key deployment-readiness steps — pinned dependencies, a post-registration smoke test, and more — completing 19 of 27 checks. With the skill, all 27 completed.

We included a skill to evaluate skills because there is no single universal “accuracy” for healthcare and life sciences workflow. For each skill, it builds a customizable evaluation harness, complete with appropriate tasks, data, scorers, and expected results and behavior, tailored to what each skill is designed to achieve. We ran and scored the evaluation tasks with and without Vital Skills.

We also tested Genie Code with and without Vital Skills three times on BiomniBench which curated tasks from top biomedical peer-reviewed papers.

  • Better where the skills apply. On the 5 tasks within the skills' scope, Genie Code's average score across 3 trials rose from 71.9 to 76.9 out of 100.
  • No cost where they don't. On 18 tasks outside the skills' scope, scores held steady — 69.1 without the skills, 71.2 with them — so the skills stay out of the way when they aren't needed.
  • The right skill, every time. With a one-line pointer to the skills in Genie Code's instructions, it opened the right one in every in-scope run.

The right skill makes the right behaviors reliable. On one cohort task, the baseline silently dropped half the eligible patients; with the skill, every one was recovered.

Previous research has shown that Genie Code is more cost-efficient than other coding agents because it uniquely understands your data on Databricks, skipping the typical random walk search.

Extend Genie Code with additional skills like Vital Skills for healthcare and life sciences tasks. Together, one can chain a myriad of skills into complex tasks. For example, after deploying open-weight models, create and schedule a batch inferencing job. If it is an embedding model, prompt Genie Code to create a vector search index.

Browse and install Vital Skills in Genie Code, Genie One or Genie Code CLI. Publish these skills to Unity Gateway to govern and share them with your coworkers. Try the ones that fit your work or customize them to suit your needs. Genie Code even helps you create new skills. Vital Skills is open source and welcomes your contributions.

entries.title: Unlocking Investment Insights Without Migrating Your Data: Lakehouse Federation
entries.summary: Lakehouse Federation: Query Anywhere, Move NothingIn today's enterprise landscape,...
entries.content:
How to combine sensitive on-premise portfolio data with third-party financial intelligence without compromising security or compliance

by Meghana Padmanabhan, Isaac Gritz and Max Nienu

  • Federate, don't copy: Databricks Lakehouse Federation queries on-premise databases directly from Databricks with standard SQL. The data never moves.
  • Subscribe, don't build: FactSet financial data from the Databricks Marketplace appears as a native catalog. No ingestion pipeline required.
  • One query, full picture: A single SQL join across both catalogs powers dashboards and Genie natural-language queries, with zero persisted intermediate objects providing rich portfolio and investment information.

In today's enterprise landscape, data rarely sits in one place. Financial institutions, asset managers, and individual investors face a common challenge: their most sensitive data including portfolio holdings, trading positions, and client information often resides in on-premises databases behind corporate firewalls, in the cloud, or across both environments. That challenge is compounded by the fact that the third-party data they need for analysis, including market data, analyst estimates, and financial fundamentals increasingly lives in the cloud.

Traditional approaches force an uncomfortable choice: copy sensitive data to the cloud, stand up brittle ETL pipelines, or give up on integrating the two altogether.

What if you could just federate the on-premises source, subscribe to the third-party data on the cloud, and go straight from those two catalogs to a dashboard and a natural-language chat, with no pipeline, no materialized views, and no persisted objects in between?

That's Databricks Lakehouse Federation at its simplest.

Databricks Lakehouse Federation lets you create federated connections to external databases like SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL, Snowflake, and more, and query them directly from Databricks using standard SQL. The data stays exactly where it is. No copying. No syncing. No compliance headaches.

Add a marketplace data share on top of it, and you have two catalogs sitting side by side in Unity Catalog - one federated, one shared, that a plain SQL query can join like they were any two ordinary tables.

Let's walk through a concrete example. Imagine you're a wealth management firm with:

  • First-party data: Your portfolio holdings - which stocks you own and how many shares, stored in an on-premises SQL Server database.
  • Third-party data: FactSet financial data from the Databricks Marketplace, including earnings fundamentals and analyst estimates.

Your goal: Build an investment dashboard that shows your projected earnings, identifies high-risk positions, and recommends actions, all without exposing your holdings data to the cloud.

Setting up federation is straightforward through the Databricks UI. Navigate to Catalog → External Data → Connections and create a new connection to your on-premises database.

The connection securely stores your credentials.

Once the connection is established, create a foreign catalog that maps to your on-premises database. This makes your external tables appear as native Unity Catalog objects.

After this step, your on-premises data appears as a catalog, but the data never leaves your SQL Server. Every query executes against the source in real time.

The Databricks Marketplace provides instant access to FactSet's comprehensive financial data. Search for FactSet, review the available datasets, and request access. Once the provider approves your request, you can subscribe to the relevant datasets.

After subscribing, the data is available as a shared catalog in your workspace, organized into schemas:

  • fe_v4 - FactSet Estimates: analyst consensus EPS forecasts, earnings projections, and estimate counts
  • ff_v3 - FactSet Fundamentals: annual financial statements including revenue, net income, profit margins, and debt levels
  • sym_v1 - Symbology: ticker-to-entity mappings that connect your portfolio symbols to FactSet's internal identifiers

These tables appear alongside your federated portfolio catalog in Unity Catalog. You can browse them, preview data, and check schemas, all without any ingestion or data copying.

With both data sources accessible through Unity Catalog, an asset manager can open the SQL editor and write one query that spans both the federated holdings on one side, the FactSet marketplace tables on the other. To the SQL author they look like two ordinary tables in the same warehouse.

There is no pipeline to author, no materialized view to schedule, and no gold layer to maintain. Every time the query runs it re-federates the on-premises source live and re-joins it against the marketplace share.

The dashboard is powered by the same combined query inlined directly into each widget's dataset. No views are created and no tables are persisted. Every widget re-federates the source on each refresh.

It instantly answers questions like:

  • Portfolio health: total holdings, current annual earnings, projected annual earnings, high-risk count
  • Risk distribution: what share of the book is high / medium / low risk?
  • Investment recommendations: how many stocks should I buy more of vs. sell?
  • Top performers: which holdings are generating the most earnings and how do current earnings compare to projected earnings?
  • Full holdings table: per-stock earnings, growth %, margin %, D/E, risk, and action recommendation.

The final piece: a Genie agent wired directly to the same federated holdings and FactSet marketplace tables. Genie receives the join chain and data-quality filters in its instructions. It translates natural language into the same queries the dashboard runs.

The result: democratized data access. Portfolio managers, financial advisors, and individual investors can all get answers without writing SQL, and without anyone materializing anything.

Databricks Lakehouse Federation fundamentally changes the economics of hybrid data analytics. Instead of the expensive, risky, and time-consuming process of moving data to the cloud, or the equally burdensome process of building and maintaining pipelines on top of it, you can bring the compute to the data and let a single query drive everything downstream.

In this example, the walkthrough built a complete investment analytics solution that:

  • Queries on-premises holdings data in real time
  • Enriches it with FactSet financial intelligence from the Marketplace
  • Combines both in a single SQL query, with no persisted intermediate objects
  • Visualizes everything in an interactive dashboard
  • Enables natural language queries with Genie

All without copying a single row of portfolio data to the cloud.

The future of data analytics isn't about moving all your data to one place and it isn't about building elaborate pipelines to reshape it either. It's about querying data wherever it lives. While this blog used investment portfolios as the example, this pattern – federate sensitive first-party data, subscribe to cloud-based third-party data, and analyze without moving or copying anything – applies broadly. Healthcare organizations can join HIPAA-protected patient records with drug interaction databases for treatment recommendations.Manufacturing firms can federate on-premises IoT telemetry with cloud-based supply chain data. Retailers can combine in-store POS systems with third-party demographic datasets.The common thread: sensitive first-party data stays protected while enabling rich analytics with third-party data.

Ready to get started? Explore the following links:

  • Set Up Federation — Follow the Lakehouse Federation documentation to connect your external databases
  • Browse the Marketplace — Browse available data products at marketplace.databricks.com
  • Create Dashboards — Use AI/BI dashboards to visualize insights
  • Enable Genie — Let your users ask questions in natural language

entries.title: From spot fixes to measured gains: improving document extraction accuracy with ai_extract and MLflow Prompt Registry
entries.summary: Document extraction often starts with a simple loop: spot an incorrect field, adjust...
entries.content:
How to improve ai_extract accuracy, version prompts and schemas, evaluate results, and how Genie Code can automate them for you

  • You don't have to do it all yourself: Genie Code for document processing automates the core of this workflow, scoring extraction field by field against your labeled data, proposing schema and instruction fixes as reviewable diffs, and re-running the eval to show before-and-after results.
  • Improve ai_extract accuracy with the right lever: Use schema descriptions for field-level rules, prompts for document-level logic, precision mode for structural complexity, and citations to diagnose errors.
  • Version prompts and schemas with MLflow Prompt Registry: Track extraction logic as versioned artifacts and deploy or roll back changes through aliases instead of editing pipeline code.
  • Evaluate changes before promotion: Compare candidates against fixed, human-reviewed ground truth while tracking accuracy, coverage, and run-to-run variation.

Document extraction often starts with a simple loop: spot an incorrect field, adjust the prompt or schema, rerun the document, and check the result.

That approach becomes unreliable as fields and document formats multiply. A change may fix one field while introducing regressions elsewhere, work for one layout but fail on another, or appear better simply due to normal variation across LLM runs.

We saw this on a recent project that extracted roughly 40 structured fields from partner-submitted order documents across dozens of PDF layouts. Reviewers corrected and approved extracted values before they moved downstream, giving us human-reviewed ground truth for evaluation.

The challenge was not getting 

ai_extract
to return the fields. It was improving extraction without degrading the system overall.

For example, the 

revision
field sometimes returned status terms such as 
ORIGINAL
instead of a 
revision
number or blank. A small schema change cut errors for that field roughly in half. But across every field, total extraction errors increased by 9%.

The lesson was clear: improving one field does not necessarily improve the extraction system.

The pipeline already had most of the pieces needed to evaluate changes systematically. Documents landed in object storage and flowed through a Lakeflow SDP pipeline using Auto Loader. Bronze parsed documents with ai_parse_document, Silver extracted structured fields with ai_extract, and Gold published results as a materialized view. Predictions synced to Lakebase, where a Databricks App let reviewers correct and approve fields, and Lakebase CDC returned those approvals to the lakehouse.

Two pieces were missing from the feedback loop. Reviewer approvals were available, but they were not assembled into a reusable evaluation dataset. At the same time, prompts and schemas were embedded directly in pipeline code, so even a small change to extraction required a code deployment.

We addressed both problems by building a workflow around three questions: What should we change? How should we version it? And what evidence is enough to promote it?

This post covers three parts of that workflow:

  • Improve ai_extract with the right lever: Use schemas for field rules, global instructions for document logic, precision mode for difficult structures, and citations to diagnose errors.
  • Version prompts and schemas: Store both in MLflow Prompt Registry and use aliases to deploy or roll back configurations without editing pipeline code.
  • Evaluate before promotion: Compare candidates on fixed, human-reviewed ground truth, tracking accuracy, coverage, and run-to-run variation.

Together, these steps create a repeatable path from a proposed extraction change to production, with evidence that the change improves the system as a whole.

The rest of this post walks through the practices we recommend and why each one matters. You don't have to implement all of them on your own. Genie Code for document processing builds the Lakeflow job (ai_parse_document, ai_classify, and ai_extract with citations and confidence scores) and automates the core of this workflow with an evaluation and hill-climbing loop:

  • Measure: Scores the current extraction field by field against your labeled table, so you can see which fields are weak.
  • Improve: Proposes a fix, most often a sharper field description, as a reviewable diff that you approve before it applies.
  • Re-evaluate: Re-runs the eval set after every accepted change and shows before-and-after results, so regressions are as visible as improvements.

For example, you can ask Genie Code: "Evaluate the extraction against my labeled table and tell me which fields are weakest," followed by "Accuracy on the revision field could be higher. Iteratively improve the schema and instructions, re-run the evaluation, and show me the before and after."

Understanding the fundamentals still matters. It helps you judge Genie Code's proposed changes, decide when a result is good enough to promote, and extend the workflow for production, for example by versioning prompts and schemas in MLflow Prompt Registry. Each section below explains a recommended practice and notes how Genie Code can handle it for you.

ai_extract
lever

ai_extract
takes three inputs: the parsed document, a JSON schema, and optional global instructions.

The schema and instructions serve different purposes:

  • Schema: Defines output fields and field-specific extraction rules.
  • Global instructions: Provide guidance that applies across the document.

The result is a structured value with one entry for each schema field. You can access individual fields directly, for example: 

extracted:response.revision.value
.

Start with the schema structure. When a field has a closed set of valid values, use an enum constraint rather than listing the allowed values in the description. Use numeric types for numbers and integers, and use nested arrays or objects for repeated structures.

Then use schema descriptions for rules that types alone cannot express, such as:

  • Preserve leading zeros in identifiers such as 
    004
  • Exclude status terms such as 
    ORIGINAL
    , 
    NEW
    , or 
    REVISED
  • Stop an identifier at the first invalid character
  • Return 
    null
    when a value isn't present

KEY: Keeping field rules in the schema makes the extraction contract easier to inspect and prevents the global prompt from becoming a list of unrelated exceptions.

Reserve the global prompt for rules that apply across the document, including:

  • Document or domain context
  • Source priority, such as headers over footers
  • Cross-field consistency rules
  • Instructions for combining rows into arrays
  • Document regions that should not be used as sources

For example, if entity names are mistakenly extracted from boilerplate footers or third-party contact blocks, a 

FORBIDDEN-SOURCES
instruction can tell the model to ignore those regions.

A useful rule is: If the rule defines one field, put it in the schema. If it defines how to interpret the document, put it in the prompt.

Automate it with Genie Code: The hill-climbing loop follows the same principle. Its proposed fixes most often sharpen a field description in the schema, and are shown as a diff for you to approve before they apply.

Not every transformation needs an LLM. Handle casing, separator removal, zero-padding, and mappings such as TELEVISION to TV with SQL or another deterministic transformation when possible.

KEY: Use the model to interpret the document; use code to normalize the output.

Sometimes the instructions are clear, but the document is difficult to follow. Large schemas, repeated line items, complex tables, and multi-page layouts can make it hard to keep values aligned with the right rows.

For these cases, 

ai_extract
version 2.1 offers precision mode:

Precision Mode brings frontier extraction capabilities for more demanding use cases. With the prompt and schema held constant, it tends to help most on repeated structures and reduces over-extraction (the model returning a value where the correct answer is blank).

Diagnose the failure before changing the configuration:

  • If the model misunderstands what a field means, change the prompt or schema.
  • If it understands the field but struggles with the data structure, test precision mode.

The approaches are complementary. In our testing, the schema rule corrected a field the model misunderstood, while precision mode improved extraction of fields from complex tables.

When an extracted value is wrong, citations help show where the model found its answer:

Citations provide field-level bounding boxes that can be mapped back to element spans in the source document. This helps distinguish between two different types of errors:

  • Extraction error: The model selected the wrong region, misunderstood the field, or returned a value that is not supported by the source.
  • Labeling disagreement: The model extracted from the correct location, but the expected answer follows a different reviewer convention.

These require different fixes. Extraction errors may call for a change to the schema or prompt. Labeling disagreements should be resolved by defining the expected convention in the reviewer guidelines.

Confidence scores can also help prioritize human review:

Use them as a ranking signal, such as reviewing low-confidence fields first, rather than as an automatic quality gate. A high-confidence result can still be wrong.

In Genie Code: The extraction tasks Genie Code builds include citations and confidence scores. You can ask it to "Set confidence thresholds per field from the evaluation results and route low-confidence rows to review," and use the Document Parsing UI to visually debug parsing and extraction.

Reduce the friction of hardcoding prompts and schemas in notebooks by managing them as configurable, reusable definitions outside the pipeline code. A small wording change requires a code deployment, previous versions are difficult to reconstruct, and there is no evidence that the new version is better than the old one.

MLflow Prompt Registry lets you version those inputs separately from pipeline code. Version both the prompt and the schema: field descriptions influence extraction just as global instructions do. Version only the prompt, and half of your extraction logic is still traveling as an untracked code change.

Beyond the Genie Code loop: Genie Code helps you find the right prompt and schema. When you take that configuration to production, versioning it lets you promote and roll back changes without a code deployment.

A simple alias strategy might use:

  • @prod
    for the currently approved version
  • @candidate
    for the version under evaluation
  • @scr_*
    for experimental versions being compared in parallel

The pipeline then loads the active versions by alias:

The resolved prompt and schema are then passed to 

ai_extract
.

When a candidate is approved, 

mlflow.genai.set_prompt_alias
can move 
@prod
to the new version. The pipeline resolves it on the next run without changing the pipeline code. To roll back, restore both aliases to the previous recorded versions. The underlying versions remain in the registry.

This separates extraction configuration from the code that runs it. Figure 2 also adds the other missing piece: reusable ground truth.

The ground-truth view pairs approved labels with source documents and predictions, creating the reference dataset for measuring changes.

Version history tells you what changed. It doesn't tell you whether the change was better. Build a fixed cohort from reviewer-approved results; ours was several hundred PDFs covering a wide range of layouts. Score the production prompt and each candidate prompt against the same test set.

For every version, track metrics such as:

  • Overall and field-level accuracy
  • Ground-truth coverage
  • Performance by document type
  • Run-to-run variation

Keep both the documents and metric definitions consistent across comparisons. Otherwise, a score change could reflect a different test set or scoring rule rather than a different extraction configuration.

In Genie Code: Point Genie Code at your labeled table, such as the ground-truth view in Figure 2, and ask it to evaluate the extraction. It scores each field and re-runs the same eval set after each accepted change, so before-and-after comparisons use the same documents. The noise-floor, coverage, and verdict checks below are useful guardrails to add when you take a change to production.

A candidate scoring slightly higher once doesn't mean it is better. Run the production configuration at least 3-5 times on the frozen test set and calculate its mean accuracy and standard deviation (σ). That σ is your noise floor. Your policy might require a candidate's improvement to exceed 2σ before treating it as meaningful; anything inside that band is inconclusive rather than a win.

Accuracy can also be misleading if you ignore missing predictions.

Suppose you score only fields where both the model and reviewer supplied a value. A candidate that leaves difficult fields blank can appear more accurate because those misses disappear from the denominator. The reverse can also happen. When we scored the 

revision
field only on documents where the reviewer supplied a 
revision
value, our fix appeared to improve accuracy by less than 3 percentage points. But when we counted all errors, including cases where the correct answer was blank, the fix cut 
revision
errors roughly in half. Most of the improvement came from correctly returning no value where one did not belong.

That is why coverage should be reported alongside accuracy. Define it explicitly, for example, as the share of non-null ground-truth fields for which the model returns a prediction. If accuracy rises but coverage falls materially, investigate before promoting the candidate.

The resulting harness follows a repeatable sequence: freeze the test set, establish the production baseline, register a candidate on a screening alias, run repeated evaluations, and compare accuracy, coverage, and stability.

Once you measure accuracy, coverage, and run-to-run variation, your evaluation harness can reduce those metrics to a small set of outcomes:

  • BETTER: Accuracy clears the predefined threshold, coverage holds, and results are stable.
  • SUSPECT: Accuracy improves, but coverage falls materially.
  • UNSTABLE: Results vary too much across runs.
  • INCONCLUSIVE: The difference is too small to distinguish from normal variation.
  • WORSE: Accuracy declines meaningfully.

These verdicts provide a consistent way to summarize an evaluation before deciding whether the candidate should be promoted to production.

We scored each candidate three times on the same test set, counting errors in every field, relative to the original prompt and schema.

Changerevision errorsErrors across all fieldsVerdict
revision
schema fix only		-49%+9%
TARGET_IMPROVED_WITH_REGRESSION
Restructured prompt and schema-57%-16%

Precision mode only, no prompt or schema change-10%-24%

Restructured prompt and schema + precision mode-64%-32%
BETTER

The spot fix did what we wanted for 

revision
, but the model started inventing values in unrelated line-item fields such as schedule details. Editing one field's description is not a one-field experiment: the model reads the schema as a whole.

So we did not ship it.

Instead, we moved field-specific rules out of the global prompt and into schema descriptions, including the same 

revision
rule. The prompt ended up at less than half its original length, and errors fell by 16% overall, with 
estimate
errors down by 30%.

Two fields worsened, and they went on the target list for the next round.

Precision mode told a different story. With no prompt or schema change, it cut errors by 24%, mostly by no longer inventing values in repeated line-item fields. But it barely changed 

revision
errors because that was a definition problem, and only the schema rule fixed it.

Combined, they stack: precision mode on top of the restructured prompt and schema removed another 19% of the remaining errors. Overall, errors fell by about a third (32%), and 

revision
errors by nearly two-thirds (64%).

This is the regression Genie Code's loop is designed to surface. Because every accepted change re-runs the full eval set, a spot fix that helps revision but hurts line-item fields appears in the before-and-after results rather than in production.

A verdict is a starting point, not the final decision.

One earlier candidate cut estimate errors by about a third and was only INCONCLUSIVE overall. But it had also started filling in a yes/no flag on nearly every document, while reviewers had marked that field on only a handful of documents.

A severe regression in one field can preclude promotion even when aggregate metrics appear acceptable. Promotion should therefore remain human-controlled.

If a candidate is classified as 

BETTER
, an owner can update the 
@prod
alias and record the candidate version, evaluation metrics, author, and timestamp.

There may also be valid reasons to promote an 

INCONCLUSIVE
change, such as implementing an important business convention not fully captured by aggregate accuracy. In those cases, recording an override reason preserves the rationale behind the decision.

With that review and alias update, the feedback loop closes:

Reliable document extraction is not about finding one perfect prompt. It is about choosing the appropriate change, tracking what changed, and testing whether the result improved.

With 

ai_extract
, that means using schema descriptions for field-level behavior, global instructions for document-level reasoning, precision mode when structure is the bottleneck, and citations when you need to understand why an extraction failed.

MLflow Prompt Registry then gives you a versioned path for managing prompts and schemas, while a fixed evaluation test set gives you evidence for deciding what should reach production.

Together, those pieces turn prompt iteration from a series of one-off edits into a repeatable engineering workflow.

Genie Code for document processing automates the core of this loop (measure, improve, re-evaluate), so most teams can start there, then add Prompt Registry versioning, noise-floor checks, and promotion gates as the pipeline moves to production.

Explore the Databricks AI Functions documentation to learn more about 

ai_extract
, and see the MLflow Prompt Registry documentation for prompt versioning and alias management. Try Genie Code for document processing. Open Genie Code from Jobs and Pipelines, point it at your documents and a labeled table, and ask it to evaluate and improve your extraction.

entries.summary: Migration as a strategic evolutionMany organizations support a range of data and analytics workloads on BigQuery today...
entries.content:
Learn a phased migration approach to adopting Databricks Lakehouse

by Takero Ibuki

  • A strategic framework for migrating from Google BigQuery to the open Databricks Lakehouse architecture
  • The framework unifies governance and consolidates BI, ETL, and multi-model AI into one environment, resulting in predictable performance and reduced operational overhead through unified workspaces
  • Lakehouse provides an "AI-ready" foundation that empowers SQL teams to build advanced data products while keeping TCO low

Many organizations support a range of data and analytics workloads on BigQuery today, but are exploring ways to bring BI, ETL, and multi-model AI workloads into a single governance and operating model. An open Lakehouse with a unified governance layer can help simplify operations, streamline compliance across data and AI, provide predictable performance as needs grow, and create a foundation for new AI-driven use cases.

A successful migration requires more than copying tables. It demands a phased strategy: moving data into open formats on services like Google Cloud Storage, transforming logic thoughtfully, and validating results with automated tooling. This guide outlines a migration framework across three pillars – Process, Technology, and People – for navigating that transition with minimal disruption and measurable business impact.

The Process pillar defines how you migrate. Success depends on choosing the right entry point and managing the transition period effectively.

The migration journey runs in sequence: assess the estate, choose an entry point, migrate, validate in dual operation, then decommission. Assessment comes before everything else: you cannot pick the right entry point without knowing what you run today. Profile the BigQuery estate first — datasets, query history and slot consumption — to find which workloads drive cost, which dashboards are actually used, and which tables are never queried at all. Lakebridge, the open-source Databricks Labs migration toolkit, includes a BigQuery profiler that automates this discovery, so migration waves are planned around what is actually used rather than what merely exists.

  • BI-first: Prioritize the dashboards decision-makers see every day. This path suits teams whose dashboards/data products need to scale and whose analysts want AI features. Rebuild the most-used dashboards on Databricks, reading BigQuery data in place at first, and switch teams over one use case at a time, proving parity side by side. The payoff is visible from day one: faster dashboards and natural-language Q&A with Genie.
  • ETL-first: Prioritize the backend when the goal is to consolidate transformation workloads onto Databricks' Photon/Spark engine and optimize cost and performance. This path suits teams that want to establish an AI-ready data foundation first and let downstream consumers such as dashboards and applications follow. The trade-off is visibility: business users see little change until pipelines land, so publish runtime and efficiency metrics with each wave. When in doubt, let the assessment decide: high dashboard usage points BI-first; heavy transformation workloads point ETL-first.

Whichever entry point you choose, migrate in waves, not in one big bang. A big-bang cutover concentrates all the risk in a single moment — and if anything breaks, so does trust in the whole program. Waves keep the blast radius small: rank workloads on two axes — value to the organization (how visible it is to leadership, how directly it touches revenue, how urgent the compliance deadline behind it is, how many people rely on it day to day) and migration complexity — and start where value is high and complexity is low. Each wave then delivers a visible business win, reconciles before the next starts, and leaves the team's playbook faster for the one after it. Reserve big bang for the rare small, low-risk estate where running two platforms costs more than it protects.

  • Lift and shift: Migrate existing SQL logic "as-is" to Databricks Lakehouse. This establishes a working baseline quickly and lets teams validate parity before optimizing.
  • Modernize: Once stable, refactor high-value pipelines into Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines for automated orchestration, built-in data quality, and a unified framework for both batch and streaming.

Most organizations navigate a Dual Operation phase using Lakehouse Federation to "shadow" workloads for validation. The key to ROI is setting clear "success criteria" (e.g., 99.9% parity) to trigger the immediate decommissioning of legacy pipelines, eliminating the cost of running two platforms.

Dual operation works in both directions, and the right bridge depends on your entry point. BI-first teams use Lakehouse Federation so Databricks can read BigQuery while dashboards move first. ETL-first teams flip it: move ingestion and transformation to Databricks, land curated tables in open formats, and let BigQuery keep serving existing dashboards and applications from that same single copy — no dual-write pipelines, no export jobs, no second copy to reconcile.

Migrating in waves keeps this dual-operation window short and narrow: only the workloads in the current wave carry the cost of running on two platforms at once, so the bill for dual operation stays proportional to what's actually in flight, not the whole estate. Treat BigQuery-as-serving-layer as a transitional state rather than a destination: the external tables are read-only on BigQuery’s side and carry limitations such as manual schema refresh after schema changes, so plan the cutover of the serving layer onto Databricks Lakehouse as the closing step of the journey.

Unity Catalog transforms governance from a hurdle into a strategic engine. It offers a seamless 3-tier mapping (Project → Catalog, Dataset → Schema, Table → Table) that replicates BigQuery permissions while adding automatic, end-to-end lineage and treating AI models as first-class citizens.

The mapping goes deeper than the object hierarchy. Unity Catalog gives you the same fine-grained protection natively: row filters restrict access row by row, and column masks and tags handle column-level security — so protection travels with the data instead of being rebuilt from scratch. And one sequencing rule from the field: migrate permissions before data, so each wave's cutover changes where a table lives, never who can see it.

The technical pillar focuses on moving data into open formats on services like Google Cloud Storage, migrating logic to Databricks SQL and Spark, and validating results.

Migrating from BigQuery to Databricks involves three workstreams: Data Migration, Logic Migration, and Validation.

Choose the path by volume and freshness. Bulk history moves fastest through BigQuery’s export to Parquet on Google Cloud Storage, usually the economical route at scale, and the export doubles as a frozen point-in-time copy that simplifies validation. Continuously updated tables are read through the Storage API connector or redirected at the source, and small, frequently changing datasets can stay queryable through federation until their wave arrives. Everything lands in open formats, ready for the medallion layers.

Never hand-convert an estate. Three tiers cover it: rule-based transpilation (e.g. Lakebridge) for the bulk of routine SQL, LLM-assisted conversion for dialect quirks, and engineers reserved for the genuinely complex tail. Orchestration follows the same pattern: scheduled queries and Composer DAGs map to Lakeflow Jobs.

Budget for validation as seriously as for the migration itself — in the field it often consumes comparable effort. Run it at three levels: completeness (row counts), consistency (schemas and types), and accuracy (aggregate reconciliation plus row-level hashing), automated with Lakebridge reconcile, which supports BigQuery as a native source. One field lesson: small built-in function differences between the two SQL dialects can break hash comparisons — investigate mismatches before assuming data loss. Parity here is what triggers decommissioning in the Process journey.

The open foundation pays off before the migration even finishes. Because Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg are open formats, the tables you land on Google Cloud Storage are readable by more than Databricks: BigQuery reads Delta through BigLake external tables and Iceberg through Iceberg external tables, and catalog federation between Unity Catalog and BigQuery (currently in preview) lets both platforms govern and query the same tables without copying them. Storage is decoupled from the engine — one copy of data, many engines. That interoperability is not a side benefit; it is the capability behind the low-risk transition patterns described in the Process section.

The third pillar provides the ultimate ROI of a migration: a more capable, unified workforce.

Ending the handoff culture. In legacy stacks, the gap between SQL Analysts and Data Scientists creates silos. In Databricks, shared Notebooks allow the entire "squad" to live in the same workspace, reducing communication overhead.

Building the new skillset. Genie acts as the bridge for SQL-heavy teams. Analysts can use natural language to generate Python or Spark code, turning traditional analysts into versatile data practitioners without a steep learning curve. Pair that day-to-day AI assist with structured training, Databricks Academy courses and role-based certifications, so the new skillset sticks organization-wide instead of depending on a few self-taught early adopters.

Engineering rigor. Teams move from "writing queries" to "building data products" by adopting software engineering best practices like Unity Catalog, Git integration and CI/CD.

Six patterns repeat across successful BigQuery migrations based on our migration project experience:

  • Profile before you plan. In most estates, a significant share of BigQuery tables are rarely or never queried. Profiling query history and slot usage first means you migrate the workloads that matter and retire the rest.
  • Define parity criteria before dual-run starts. Agree the success threshold (for example, 99.9% reconciliation across row counts, aggregates and hashes) up front — without it, the shadow period has no exit condition.
  • Don’t hand-convert SQL. Rule-based transpilation plus AI-assisted conversion handles the bulk of the estate; reserve engineers for the genuinely complex remainder.
  • Map governance one-to-one first, modernize second. The project → catalog, dataset → schema, table → table mapping into Unity Catalog preserves existing permissions — including row- and column-level policies — on day one; richer tagging, attribute-based controls and lineage-driven governance can evolve after cutover.
  • Treat BI-first as a change-management project. The technology is often the easier half; the analysts whose dashboards move need enablement, champions and a feedback loop.
  • Right-size your platform footprint. Once workloads are validated on Databricks, retire duplicated processing to avoid running and paying for the same work in two places (“double bubble”). Celebrate completed migrations, not just go-lives.

Migrating to Databricks isn't one leap — it's a sequence of decisions you can actually plan for: which entry point fits your team, how to sequence waves so each one banks a win before the next starts, and which bridge keeps BigQuery and Databricks running side by side until the last dashboard cuts over. Get that sequencing right, and Process, Technology, and People reinforce each other: data migration, logic transformation, and validation retire the estate on one side, while analysts querying in natural language with Genie and engineers shipping governed data products build on it on the other.

The result is an open lakehouse, a migration your organization can trust wave over wave, and a team that's ready to build on what it lands on.

Ready to plan your migration? Explore the Databricks migration hub, assess your estate with the open-source Lakebridge toolkit, or contact your Databricks account team for a migration assessment.

Bring your docs, tickets, emails, and AI tools into a single, governed foundation with Lakeflow Connect to fuel AI agents and Genie analytics

by Sonia Bendre and Giselle Goicochea

  • Productivity and collaboration tools hold your most valuable enterprise knowledge, but this data has been historically siloed across dozens of separate applications, behind a custom API integration for every source.
  • Lakeflow Connect provides native, fully managed connectors for Atlassian (Jira, Confluence), Microsoft (SharePoint, Outlook), Google Workspace (Drive, Gmail), GitHub, and major AI providers (OpenAI, Anthropic) with unified governance and no infrastructure to manage.
  • Since both unstructured and structured data lands directly in Unity Catalog, data teams can easily power enterprise knowledge bases, AI agents and developer productivity dashboards without building or maintaining custom data pipelines.

This is the second post in our series on how Lakeflow Connect brings fully managed data ingestion to every line of business. Following our deep dive into unifying marketing data, this post focuses on unlocking the enterprise knowledge trapped within your organization's productivity stack. We’ll explore how native connectors for wikis, project management tools, and AI foundation models give your downstream AI agents the complete business context they need.

Lakeflow Connect provides a comprehensive suite of fully managed native connectors across SaaS applications, databases, and file sources that ingest your data directly into the Databricks Platform. Each connector can be set up via a point-and-click UI or a simple API. From there, your data is incrementally ingested as governed, managed tables in Unity Catalog, with no infrastructure for you to provision, manage, or scale.

Prioritized by customer demand, Lakeflow Connect's ingestion connectors span every line of business, including Customer 360, Operations, Finance, and Productivity—the stack closest to day-to-day work.

The average company's productivity stack is a sprawl of project trackers, wikis, document stores, inboxes, and AI tools, each holding only a slice of how work gets done. Getting that data out has historically required a patchwork of custom pipelines that are slow to build and painful to maintain. The bar is high enough that the most impactful use cases stay out of reach, for example: AI agents powered by your enterprise's internal knowledge or visibility into operational analytics.

Lakeflow Connect resolves this by providing built-in connectors to ingest seamlessly from across the productivity stack:

  • COLLABORATION: How does work get tracked and shipped? Jira, Monday.com, Smartsheet, Aha!, and GitHub
  • ENTERPRISE KNOWLEDGE: What collective expertise does your company run on? Confluence, Notion, Glean, SharePoint, and Google Drive
  • EMAIL: How do your teams communicate? Outlook and Gmail
  • AI: How is your organization adopting AI? OpenAI and Anthropic

With this breadth of connectors, Lakeflow Connect becomes the ingestion engine that brings scattered productivity data into one governed foundation, without the integration bottlenecks that traditionally slow teams down.

For example, Toyota Finance Australia, the financing arm of one of the world's largest automakers, uses Lakeflow Connect to bring its Jira data into Databricks as a fully managed, zero-maintenance pipeline.

“Lakeflow Connect for Jira has transformed how we onboard and consume Jira data within our enterprise data management platform. Moving to the fully managed, UI-driven experience offered by Databricks provided a seamless, zero-maintenance pipeline that automatically handles API complexity and schema changes while delivering governed, analytics-ready Delta tables in the Databricks Lakehouse with minimal effort and maximum reliability.”- Charbel Khoury, Head of Data Office, Toyota Finance Australia Limited

Similarly, Seguros SURA, uses the Monday.com connector to turn isolated task boards into governed, enterprise-ready insights..

"Using the Monday.com connector from Lakeflow Connect, we can centralize project and operations data that previously lived scattered across different boards into Databricks. Thanks to automatic synchronization, we no longer deal with manual exports or outdated data. By uniting this information with our other business data on the same platform, we can easily build more complete analyses, with governance and access control managed by Unity Catalog."- Juan David Munera, Head of Data and AI, Seguros Sura Mexico

VaxCare, a vaccine management company runs the largest primary-care vaccination network in the U.S., and uses Lakeflow Connect's Confluence connector to feed its internal knowledge base into Databricks and ground an AI agent in it.

"Lakeflow Connect's Confluence connector gives us a seamless way to feed our internal knowledge base into Databricks, making that data searchable and actionable for our chatbot today—and ready to power future AI solutions as we build them." - Yasaman Malone, VP of Optimization and AI, VaxCare

AI agents can provide instant, grounded answers from your company's collective knowledge without employees having to hunt across wikis, drives, and inboxes. But an agent is only as good as the data behind it, and most of that is unstructured. With Lakeflow Connect, this is not a problem; our connectors can land unstructured content like files, pages, and messages as governed tables in Unity Catalog. The exact data, and the format it arrives in, varies by source:

  • SharePoint: The SharePoint connector brings in the unstructured files themselves (PDFs, Word documents, slide decks, and images). Each unstructured file lands as one row, with its raw bytes stored in a 
    content
    column (either as 
    BINARY
     or 
    FILE
     type), with per-file metadata stored alongside. Structured files (Excel files, CSVs, etc.) can also be landed directly as Delta tables. 
  • Google Drive: The Google Drive connector works the same way for unstructured files, landing each document’s raw bytes as one row in a 
    content
    column. Structured files (Google Sheets, CSVs, etc.) can also be landed directly as Delta tables. 
  • Confluence: The Confluence connector brings in the content of every page and blog post as 
    STRUCT
     type in a 
    body
    field of the 
    pages
    and 
    blogposts
    tables. 
  • Outlook: The Outlook connector stores the email body in a 
    full_body_content
    column as a text string (either HTML or plain text), and it stores the attachments in an 
    attachments
    column as 
    BINARY
     type. Both live in the 
    email_messages
    table.
  • Gmail: The Gmail connector brings in the full message body as a text string, held in the 
    messages
    table. It also ingests a reference to each attachment as an 
    attachmentId
    .
  • GitHub: The GitHub connector brings in repository text files (source code, Markdown, and config), stored in the 
    content
    column of the 
    repo_contents
    table.

Whatever the source, the content lands in Unity Catalog as a governed table, where you can begin to transform it for downstream AI use cases.

  • Text that comes in (like Confluence pages, email bodies, and GitHub source files) is ready to chunk and embed after light cleanup.
  • On the other hand, document files that arrive as raw bytes (like the files from SharePoint and Google Drive or the attachments from Outlook), are first turned into text with 
    ai_parse_document
    , Databricks' built-in document intelligence.

Either way you end up with text you can index for retrieval and put behind an agent. For a deeper look at document processing, watch this on-demand session, Intelligent Document Processing with Lakeflow; and for more on how to get started, read the downstream RAG guide.

entries.content:
A practical guide for faculty: map your courses to the right tools, distribute assignments, and get students building on real production data and AI infrastructure, for free.

by Joey Frazee and Elise Hollowed

  • One platform can support an entire data + AI curriculum, from introductory data science and statistics through data engineering, BI, machine learning, AI, and capstone projects.
  • The learning experience is closer to real-world practice: students use Apache Spark, Delta Lake, MLflow, Lakebase, Genie, Databricks Apps, and other industry tools rather than learning a separate classroom-only stack.
  • Adoption is designed to be lightweight for instructors: assignments can be distributed through an existing LMS or GitHub, students can collaborate in shared notebooks, and datasets can be distributed through cloud storage, Open Sharing, or Marketplace.

You can run a full data or AI course on the same platform enterprises use in production - for free, with no cloud contract, no license to manage, and nothing to install. Databricks Free Edition is a perpetually free version of the platform; each student signs up individually and works entirely in the browser, so a course can adopt it without provisioning servers or purchasing anything.

Data and AI skills are moving faster than most curricula can follow, and the demand for these skills is showing up in both hiring and learner behavior. LinkedIn named Databricks one of its Top 10 Skills on the Rise for 2026, while Udemy included Databricks among its 100 Fastest-Growing Global Skills. Two very different signals pointing in the same direction: knowing how to work with modern data and AI platforms is increasingly valuable.

For a student, that can be the difference between “I've studied distributed computing” and “I've built a data pipeline on the platform your team uses.” For an instructor, it means making an existing course more directly connected to how data and AI work gets done in industry, without fully redesigning the curriculum.

The barriers that often make industry platforms difficult to bring into the classroom, including cost, licensing, and IT provisioning, are solved by Databricks Free Edition; a permanently free account with no credit card, no cloud contract, and nothing to install.

That matters because the two usual barriers to teaching with industry tools are cost and setup, and Free Edition removes both. It’s designed specifically for learning and non-commercial use, and is available to students and educators globally.

What is Databricks Free Edition? A no-cost, perpetually free version of the Databricks Data + AI Platform, built for students, hobbyists, and aspiring data and AI professionals. It runs in the browser with no cloud contract and no credit card required to sign up, on smaller compute sizes under fair-use limits. It is not for production or commercial use. (Source: databricks.com/learn/free-edition)

Databricks also has deep roots in academia. It was founded by the UC Berkeley professors and PhD students who created Apache Spark™, and open source is still at the center of what we build - Delta Lake, MLflow, and Unity Catalog are developed with global communities under vendor-neutral foundations (the Linux Foundation, LF AI & Data, and the Apache Software Foundation), and Databricks recently open sourced Omnigent, a meta-harness for AI agents. For educators, that means the skills students build are rooted in industry-wide open standards, not a single proprietary tool.

Because Free Edition is the real platform rather than a simplified sandbox, the skills transfer directly. A student who writes a Spark job, runs a SQL query, deploys a model, or builds an agent in Free Edition is using the same tools professionals use in production. There's no "now unlearn the training tool and learn the real one" step later.

One environment can serve as a statistics lab, a database course, a business-analytics class, and an AI capstone - which cuts the number of tools students and instructors have to learn. This table maps common courses to the tools that might fit your current curriculum.

Capstones, software-engineering projects, student builds and hackathons Databricks Apps Build and deploy interactive data and AI applications Building Enterprise Applications with Databricks Apps

Across these surfaces, Genie Code, the platform's agentic coding and data assistant, helps students generate, explain, and debug code and take on multi-step tasks autonomously, reflecting how work is increasingly done.

Distribute through your existing LMS or a GitHub repository. Export the assignment notebook as an 

.ipynb
file and share it with any datasets or instructions; students import a copy into their Free Edition workspace, complete it, and export the finished notebook for submission. For group assignments, students can share a notebook and collaborate in real time.

Three options for datasets too large for GitHub or a local download: (1) host the dataset in cloud storage students connect to; (2) use Open Sharing to share the dataset from your Free Edition workspace directly into each student's workspace; or (3) pick a free dataset from Databricks Marketplace that students access natively inside the platform.

Yes. Databricks is built for collaboration — with real-time co-authoring, comments, and tagging, students can work together and invite you into their notebooks to troubleshoot or give feedback. Databricks Free Edition is designed for up to five people to share an account for a group project. See how to set up collaboration in Databricks Free Edition.

Free Edition runs on smaller compute sizes under fair-use limits. If a workspace exceeds its quota, its compute pauses for the rest of the day and resumes the next day. Hitting a limit mid-assignment is rare and never permanent. Furthermore, you and your students can double your available daily credit up to three times per year, so students can always keep working during crunch periods and exams. The best way to ensure a smooth experience is to test each assignment in Free Edition ahead of time to catch any step that needs significant compute.

Yes - it's perpetually free, with no cloud contract and no credit card required to sign up. It's built for learning and explicitly not for production or commercial use, which fits a classroom well. Credits reset daily, so students start each day fresh.

A good place to start is anywhere you currently use a cloud-based notebook environment. Sign up for Databricks Free Edition yourself and take the Databricks Fundamentals course; once you're comfortable, assign both to your students and see how the self-paced courses fit your existing curriculum.
